newsitem.title: UK: Major urges parents keep school crisis in perspective.
newsitem.headline: Major urges parents keep school crisis in perspective.

text.p: British classrooms, once bastions of order, have been hit by a discipline crisis with the latest focus of concern a school closed after pupils attacked teachers.
But Prime Minister John Major on Friday urged parents to keep the emotive issue in perspective and promised to re-establish control promptly at one rogue school.
The Ridings School in Halifax, northern England was closed by local authorities on Thursday after reports of the assaults on teachers. Teachers voted overwhelmingly to strike.
Unions for the embattled teachers said a woman teacher was sexually assaulted while a male teacher was punched in the face.
The assaults came after the government sent in an inspection team to the school at the centre of a nationwide debate about morality. It will reopen next week with a new headmaster.
Major said the discipline breakdown would be dealt with promptly and comprehensively.

"I hope, however, that people will keep the issue of this school in proper perspective. The vast majority of schools in the state system are in good order," he insisted in an interview with the Press Association news agency.

Every outburst of classroom anarchy is being put under the microscope by politicians fighting for the moral high ground in the run-up to a general election. They and the media play up fears that social values are breaking down.
Right-wingers want caning brought back in schools and pupils may be taught a morality code in a bid to bring order back.
Education has become an emotionally charged battlefield for politicians in the runup to the next election, due by next May.
Frances Lawrence, the wife of a London headmaster stabbed to death by a teenage thug, struck a chord with Britons when she urged a new morality code in a country hit by rising violence.
An opinion poll in The London Times on Friday showed that Britons are now more worried about crime and than unemployment.
Twice as many people thought the opposition Labour Party was more likely than the ruling Conservatives to tackle violence along the lines put forward by Lawrence.
Education Secretary Gillian Shephard, at the eye of the classroom storm, was publicly rebuked this week by Major when she supported a return to caning, banned in Britain in 1985.
Major, whose own "back to basics" morality campaign badly misfired amid sleaze allegations, said the government had no intention of bringing back corporal punishment.
Morality is now headline news in a country where politicians, parents and teachers fear they have lost their self-confidence and sense of moral direction.

New legislation will ban virtually all handguns after 16 Scottish schoolchildren and their teacher were murdered by a lone gunman, and pressure is building for cross-party consensus on banning all combat knives after Thomas Lawrence's death.
